lessons.title: Data types, stem-and-leaf diagrams and quartiles
lessons.summary: Choose a suitable representation, preserve every observation and read values and quartiles from an explicit key.
lessons.objective: Choose a suitable representation, preserve every observation and read values and quartiles from an explicit key.
lessons.before: Read scales, order numerical data and calculate with exact fractions.
lessons.ideas:
Start with the variable

Categories such as colours are qualitative. Counts are discrete quantitative data. A measurement such as mass is continuous even when rounded before recording. A numerical label, such as a bus route number, is not a measured quantity.

A stem and a leaf form one value

Place stems vertically in order and leaves horizontally in order. Retain repetitions and empty intermediate stems. Choose a unit and a key; the same digits can represent different scales. For example, \(2\mid3\) could mean 23 minutes or 2.3 grams.

StemLeaves
12 7 7
21 4 8
32

Key: \(2\mid3\) represents \(23\) minutes.

Read ordered positions, not the visual width alone

Count every leaf. For odd n the median is observation \((n+1)/2\); for even n average the middle two. In this chapter, raw-data quartiles are medians of the two halves, excluding the overall median when n is odd. State this convention when another method is possible.

\[\mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1.\]

A representation has a purpose

A stem diagram preserves individual small-sample values; a histogram summarises a grouped distribution. A truncated bar-chart baseline can exaggerate a comparison. Choose a diagram that answers the question, and explain what information it retains or loses.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the variable, units and any measurement rounding.
  2. Read the key, scale and relevant convention before calculating.
  3. Keep repeated observations and distinguish raw values from grouped estimates.
  4. Give a complete result and compare centre and spread in context.
mistakes: A leaf is a digit, not a whole observation; read the key.
A histogram area, not its height alone, represents frequency.
Grouped quartiles are estimates; raw-data conventions must be stated.
A diagram alone does not determine every original observation or its exact mean.

examples.title: Preserve both copies of a repeated value
examples.question: Display these durations in minutes: 12, 17, 17, 21, 24, 28, 32. Include a key.
examples.solution:
StemLeaves
12 7 7
21 4 8
32

Key: \(2\mid3\) represents \(23\) minutes.

There are seven leaves, including two copies of 17. The rows represent equal-width tens classes.

examples.title: Read the measurement unit, not just the digits
examples.question: A key says \(4\mid7\) represents 4.7 g. Interpret \(6\mid2\) and \(10\mid5\).
examples.solution: The values are 6.2 g and 10.5 g. The stem holds all digits before the tenths leaf; it is not restricted to one digit.

examples.title: Find quartiles from the ordered positions
examples.question: Find the median and IQR of 12, 17, 17, 21, 24, 28, 32. Exclude the overall median when splitting the halves.
examples.solution:
The middle observation is 21. The lower half is 12, 17, 17 and the upper half is 24, 28, 32.

\[Q_1=17,\quad Q_2=21,\quad Q_3=28,\quad\mathrm{IQR}=11.\]

examples.title: A count and a rounded measurement differ
examples.question: A survey records the number of journeys and a parcel mass to the nearest gram. Classify the underlying variables.
examples.solution: The journey count is discrete quantitative data. The mass is continuous quantitative data; rounding changes the recorded precision, not the underlying type.

lessons.title: Back-to-back diagrams, comparisons and missing values
lessons.summary: Read mirrored leaves correctly and combine numerical comparisons with the meaning of the variable.
lessons.objective: Read mirrored leaves correctly and combine numerical comparisons with the meaning of the variable.
lessons.before: Read scales, order numerical data and calculate with exact fractions.
lessons.ideas:
Both samples share the stems

On the right, values increase away from the stem to the right. On the left, the smallest leaf is nearest the stem, so the displayed row descends from left to right. Each side must retain its own repetitions and sample size. Give a two-sided key.

Route AStemRoute B
8 4 211 6 9
9 6 4 123 5
—31 4

Key: \(4\mid2\mid3\) represents \(24\) minutes for Route A and \(23\) minutes for Route B.

Compare a centre and a spread

Name the samples, statistic and context. A lower median completion time means a typical job took less time; a smaller IQR means the middle half was more consistent. A smaller median does not imply smaller spread.

Missing observations use the right total

\[\text{sum}=n\bar{x}.\]

After adding a value, increase n as well as the sum. When the task supplies summary statistics for two samples, reconstruct totals before combining them:

\[\sum x^2=n(\sigma^2+\bar{x}^{\,2}),\qquad\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar{x}^{\,2}.\]

These are descriptive statistics with divisor n. Some written problems use mean/SD material from the next two book chapters; they are labelled as mixed-topic practice.

examples.question:
Interpret the back-to-back diagram and compare the routes.

Route AStemRoute B

9 6 4 123 5
—31 4

Key: \(4\mid2\mid3\) represents \(24\) minutes for Route A and \(23\) minutes for Route B.
examples.solution: Route A has median 21 and IQR 12 minutes. Route B has median 23 and IQR 15 minutes. A typically took less time and its middle half was less spread out. The left rows are read from the stem outwards, not as ascending left-to-right rows.

examples.title: Update the count before finding a missing value
examples.question: Four values are 7, 9, 10 and 14. After one more value is included, the mean is 11. Find it.
examples.solution:
\[x=5(11)-(7+9+10+14)=15.\]

The final total contains five observations, not four.

examples.title: Equal IQR does not imply equal range
examples.question: A has five-number summary \((2,6,10,14,40)\); B has \((4,7,12,15,25)\). Compare centre, IQR and range.
examples.solution: A has a lower median, 10 rather than 12. Both IQRs are 8, so the middle halves have equal spread. Their ranges are 38 and 21; A has more extreme overall spread. These comparisons do not determine their exact means.

examples.title: Combine totals, not standard deviations
examples.question: A sample of 3 has mean 10 and population SD 2; another of 2 has mean 15 and population SD 3. Find the combined mean and variance.
examples.solution:
\[\sum x=3(10)+2(15)=60,\quad\sum x^2=3(104)+2(234)=780.\]\[\bar{x}=12,\qquad\sigma^2=\frac{780}{5}-12^2=12.\]

The SDs themselves are not averaged.

lessons.title: Histograms, class boundaries and grouped estimates
lessons.summary: Use bar area as frequency, respect unequal class widths and distinguish exact records from midpoint estimates.
lessons.objective: Use bar area as frequency, respect unequal class widths and distinguish exact records from midpoint estimates.
lessons.before: Read scales, order numerical data and calculate with exact fractions.
lessons.ideas:
Frequency is proportional to bar area

\[\text{frequency density}=\frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}.\]

A class twice as wide need not have twice the height. Adjacent continuous classes touch. Label both axes and show the density scale; the tallest bar need not be the most frequent class.

Rounding determines continuous boundaries

Values recorded to the nearest unit from 20 through 29 occupy \([19.5,29.5)\) under the stated half-up rounding convention. Values recorded to the nearest tenth need a half-tenth adjustment, not a half-unit adjustment.

A physical height is not yet a frequency

If one vertical centimetre represents k density units, multiply the physical height by k, then multiply by class width. Keep horizontal and vertical scale factors separate.

Midpoints give a model, not recovered raw data

\[\bar{x}\approx\frac{\sum fm}{\sum f},\qquad\sigma\approx\sqrt{\frac{\sum fm^2}{\sum f}-\bar{x}^{\,2}}.\]

Here m is a class midpoint. The results are estimates because the individual positions inside each class are unknown. Correcting a raw observation within the same class need not change these grouped estimates, while the exact raw-data statistics can change.

  4. Give a complete result and compare centre and spread in context.

examples.title: A continuous boundary lies between rounded readings
examples.question: Lengths recorded to the nearest 0.1 cm are grouped from 2.0 through 2.9 cm. Give the continuous boundaries and width.
examples.solution:
\[1.95\le x<2.95,\qquad\text{width}=1.\]

The boundaries are half a recording unit beyond the first and last recorded values.

examples.title: Recover frequency from a plotted height
examples.question: A width-5 class has a bar 3 cm high. The vertical scale is 2 density units per centimetre. Find its frequency.
examples.solution:
\[\text{density}=3(2)=6,\qquad f=5(6)=30.\]

The plotted height must first be converted using the vertical scale.

examples.title: A midpoint calculation is an estimate
examples.question: Classes \([0,10),[10,20),[20,40)\) have frequencies 2, 4 and 4. Find the midpoint estimates of the mean and population variance.
examples.solution:
\[\sum f=10,\quad\sum fm=190,\quad\sum fm^2=4550.\]\[\bar{x}\approx19,\qquad\sigma^2\approx455-19^2=94.\]

The estimated SD is \(\sqrt{94}\). Actual within-class values need not have these exact statistics.

lessons.title: Cumulative frequency graphs, quartiles and percentiles
lessons.summary: Build cumulative totals at class boundaries and distinguish forward counts from inverse percentile readings.
lessons.objective: Build cumulative totals at class boundaries and distinguish forward counts from inverse percentile readings.
lessons.before: Read scales, order numerical data and calculate with exact fractions.
lessons.ideas:
Plot cumulative counts at upper boundaries

Begin at the first lower boundary with cumulative frequency zero. Add frequencies in order and plot at successive upper boundaries. The graph must not decrease. Join points with an appropriate increasing curve; a straight-line model is stated explicitly in the exact short checks.

Read a quantile across, then down

For N observations, read quartiles at cumulative levels \(N/4,N/2,3N/4\). A grouped graph gives estimates rather than exact ordered raw observations. For a stated straight-line segment,

\[x=L+\frac{r-C_{\rm before}}{f}\,w.\]

Here r is the target cumulative count, f the class frequency and w its width. Do not confuse cumulative frequency with class frequency.

A tail is a complement

If C(a) is the estimated count below a, the estimated count above a is \(N-C(a)\). The count between a and b is \(C(b)-C(a)\), not the difference of the measurement values. Divide a count by N before converting to a percentage.

An inverse percentile starts with the frequency axis

For the 80th percentile, locate \(0.8N\) first; 80 itself is generally neither the measurement nor the count. Reasonable readings of a carefully drawn freehand curve remain a matter for marking judgement in written questions.

examples.solution: Successive differences give 12, 16 and 12; the final cumulative total is 40. The middle cumulative value 28 is not the second class frequency.

examples.title: Interpolate a median on a stated straight segment
examples.question: Use the displayed cumulative points joined by straight segments. Estimate the median.
examples.solution:
\[r=20,\qquad Q_2=10+\frac{20-12}{16}(10)=15.\]

The measurement lies halfway through the middle class in this model; it is not the twentieth raw observation read from a list.

examples.title: Convert the upper tail into a percentage
examples.question: For the same model, estimate the percentage above 30.
examples.solution:
Between 20 and 40 the cumulative total rises from 28 to 40, so at 30 it is 34.

\[\frac{40-34}{40}(100)=15\%.\]

examples.title: Invert a percentile reading
examples.question: For the same straight-line model, estimate the 80th percentile.
examples.solution:
\[r=0.8(40)=32,\qquad x=20+\frac{32-28}{12}(20)=\frac{80}{3}.\]

The result is a measurement estimate, about 26.7, not the cumulative count 32.

lessons.title: Box-and-whisker plots, outliers and interpretation
lessons.summary: Find a complete five-number summary, follow the stated whisker rule and make defensible comparisons.
lessons.objective: Find a complete five-number summary, follow the stated whisker rule and make defensible comparisons.
lessons.before: Read scales, order numerical data and calculate with exact fractions.
lessons.ideas:
A box shows the middle half

The five-number summary is minimum, \(Q_1\), median, \(Q_3\), maximum. The box extends from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_3\); its internal line marks the median. Use one shared measurement scale when comparing samples.

State both quartile and whisker conventions

Raw quartiles here are medians of the halves, excluding an odd-sample overall median. Unless a question says otherwise, whiskers reach the minimum and maximum, including outliers. The rule must not silently change to a different boxplot convention.

Outlier fences identify unusual observations

\[Q_1-1.5\mathrm{IQR},\qquad Q_3+1.5\mathrm{IQR}.\]

An observation strictly outside these fences is an outlier under this rule. A fence need not be an observed value and is not automatically a whisker endpoint.

Compare only what the diagram supports

Compare medians and IQRs in context; use range if total spread is relevant. A boxplot does not determine the exact mean, every raw value, or prove a normal model. One written family uses later normal-model vocabulary and is clearly labelled as a later-topic application.

examples.title: Locate five ordered landmarks
examples.question: Find a five-number summary for 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 11, 13, 16, 25, using the chapter convention.
examples.solution:
\[\min=2,\quad Q_1=4.5,\quad Q_2=8,\quad Q_3=14.5,\quad\max=25.\]

The overall median 8 is excluded from both halves. The IQR is 10.

examples.title: A fence is not a replacement observation
examples.question: Given \(Q_1=4,Q_3=12\), minimum 1 and maximum 30, identify outliers and whisker endpoints under the min/max convention.
examples.solution:
\[\mathrm{IQR}=8,\qquad\text{fences}=-8,24.\]

The value 30 is an outlier. Under the stated convention the whiskers still end at 1 and 30; neither fence is substituted as an observation.

examples.title: A higher median and a smaller IQR are separate facts
examples.question: A has median 18 and IQR 7; B has median 16 and IQR 11. The variable is completion time in minutes. Compare.
examples.solution: A has a higher typical completion time, so it typically took longer. Its middle half is less spread out, so those times were more consistent. It is possible to be more consistent while being slower.

examples.title: Do not infer a missing mean
examples.question: A boxplot has five-number summary \((5,10,14,20,80)\). Can its exact mean be found? Which summary is resistant to the extreme upper value?
examples.solution: The five landmarks do not specify all observations, so the exact mean cannot be recovered. Median and IQR describe the centre and middle-half spread without being directly driven by the size of the extreme maximum. A normal model is not established by this summary.

(a) The A median is in \(31<t\leq46\); the B median is in \(46<t\leq76\).

(b) \(31\)

(c) \(41.6\)

(a)

The median position is \(62\). For Process A this lies between cumulative frequencies 46 and 84. For Process B it lies between 43 and 78. Therefore the B median lies in a strictly later, non-overlapping class.

(b)

Subtract the cumulative count at the lower boundary from the count at the upper boundary.

\[46-15=31.\]

(c)

(a) \(40\) and \(23.4\).

(b) Approximately 98.

(c) \(75\) cm
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The lower quartile is at cumulative frequency \(50\). Linear interpolation in the interval \(30<x\leq40\) gives

\[30+\frac{50-44}{56}(40-30)=\frac{435}{14}\approx 31.1.\]

Accept a sensible graph reading within the stated plotting tolerance.

The median is at cumulative frequency \(100\). Linear interpolation in the interval \(30<x\leq40\) gives

\[30+\frac{100-44}{56}(40-30)=40\approx 40.\]

Accept a sensible graph reading within the stated plotting tolerance.

The upper quartile is at cumulative frequency \(150\). Linear interpolation in the interval \(40<x\leq55\) gives

\[40+\frac{150-100}{52}(55-40)=\frac{1415}{26}\approx 54.4.\]

Accept a sensible graph reading within the stated plotting tolerance.

\[\mathrm{IQR}\approx 23.4.\]

(b)

Read both cumulative frequencies and subtract the lower reading from the upper reading.

\[127.73-30\approx 98.\]

(c)

The required cumulative proportion is 94%, not 6%.

Required value is at cumulative frequency \(188\). Linear interpolation in the interval \(70<x\leq90\) gives

\[70+\frac{188-184}{16}(90-70)=75\approx 75.\]

Accept a sensible graph reading within the stated plotting tolerance.
